subsections.subsection_title: Microbial Leakage and Periapical Inflammation Background
subsections.content:
The biological rationale for evaluating Resilon is rooted in the well-established link between microbial persistence or re-entry and apical periodontitis. Endodontic treatment succeeds when the canal system is sufficiently disinfected and then sealed against reinfection; conversely, coronal or apical leakage can permit nutrient influx and bacterial colonization, sustaining periapical inflammation. Classic experimental and clinical work has therefore framed obturation not merely as space filling, but as a barrier function whose quality influences post-treatment disease development and healing.

Within this context, Shipper et al. used a dog coronal leakage model to compare gutta-percha/AH26 with the Resilon–Epiphany system after repeated microbial inoculation. Histologically, roots filled with Resilon exhibited substantially less periapical inflammation than roots filled with gutta-percha/AH26, while negative controls remained largely uninflamed, supporting the view that improved resistance to coronal microleakage can translate into reduced apical pathosis in vivo [1]. This study became influential because it connected leakage performance to a biologically meaningful endpoint—periapical inflammation—rather than relying solely on dye or fluid transport surrogates [1].

For a literature review on Resilon, this background is essential because many subsequent claims of superiority were built on the premise that a bonded obturation or so-called monoblock could better resist bacterial penetration than conventional gutta-percha/sealer combinations. At the same time, the microbial-leakage paradigm also highlights the need to distinguish short-term sealing performance from durable clinical protection: even if early leakage is reduced, long-term anti-inflammatory benefit depends on the stability of the sealer–dentin and core–sealer interfaces under functional and hydrolytic challenge. This tension between initial microbial resistance and sustained biologic performance motivates the later discussion of material degradation and handling-related obturation quality [1].

Because Resilon is based on polycaprolactone (PCL), its long-term stability is fundamentally different from that of gutta-percha. PCL contains hydrolysable ester linkages, making the material potentially vulnerable to aqueous and enzyme-mediated breakdown in ways that conventional gutta-percha is not. This issue is central to endodontic performance because degradation may progressively alter surface integrity, interfacial adaptation, and the persistence of the obturating mass under clinical conditions ref [2].

Experimental degradation studies support this concern. In enzymatic media, Resilon exhibited surface thinning, matrix dissolution, and measurable weight loss, whereas gutta-percha showed only slight weight gain attributable mainly to fluid sorption. Tay and co-workers demonstrated that both lipase and cholesterol esterase could attack the Resilon/PCL matrix, exposing embedded filler particles and generating a roughened surface morphology consistent with ester-bond cleavage and polymer erosion ref [2]. These findings indicate that hydrolytic susceptibility is not merely theoretical but can be induced under biologically relevant catalytic conditions.

A complementary in vitro degradation analysis likewise showed that Resilon undergoes an initial water uptake followed by mass loss in aqueous media, accompanied by limited ion release, principally sodium and calcium. Compared with phosphate glass/PCL experimental composites, Resilon produced only faint surface residue and did not show the same degree of surface precipitate formation that might otherwise offset degradative changes at the material-fluid interface ref [3]. Taken together, the available evidence suggests that Resilon’s biodegradable polyester chemistry may compromise hydrolytic stability over time, and that degradation products and surface alterations should be considered when interpreting its sealing durability and clinical longevity ref [2], ref [3].

subsections.subsection_title: Thermoplastic Handling Properties of Obturation Materials
subsections.content:
Thermoplastic handling is a clinically important attribute for obturation materials because it influences flow, adaptation to canal irregularities, and suitability for warm vertical compaction or injectable techniques. Within the Resilon literature, comparative bench studies consistently positioned the material as at least as flowable as, and often more thermoplastic than, conventional gutta-percha formulations. In a standardized compression model after heating at 70°C, Resilon exhibited the greatest increase in specimen area among the tested materials, exceeding both conventional and thermoplastic gutta-percha cones from different manufacturers, which supported its characterization as a readily plasticized obturation polymer under heat ref [4].

This favorable plasticization profile was also confirmed under device-based heating conditions that more closely approximate clinical thermoplastic delivery. Using the Obtura II system, Tanomaru-Filho et al. showed that measured extrusion temperatures were substantially lower than nominal device settings, yet material-dependent differences in plasticization remained evident: at intermediate temperature settings, Resilon performed among the most thermoplastic materials, and at the highest setting it showed the greatest mean thermoplasticity of all groups tested ref [5]. These findings suggest that Resilon can achieve substantial softening within the practical thermal range used for injectable obturation, potentially facilitating canal wall adaptation and filling of accessory anatomy.

From a handling perspective, however, greater thermoplasticity should not be interpreted as an unqualified advantage. Increased heat-softening may improve flow and ease of placement, but it also raises technique-sensitive questions regarding extrusion control, dimensional behavior during cooling, and the balance between flowability and cohesive mass formation. Thus, in the background of Resilon’s development, its thermoplastic behavior was generally viewed as a favorable practical property relative to many gutta-percha cones, while still requiring consideration alongside sealing strategy, retreatability, and long-term material stability ref [4], ref [5].

subsections.section_title: Interfacial Sealing Performance and Microleakage Assessment
subsections.subsection_title: Apical Seal and Ultrastructural Interface Evaluation
subsections.content:
Early claims that Resilon/Epiphany could create a so-called monoblock at the apical end have not been fully supported by ultrastructural evidence. In a seminal SEM/TEM study, Tay et al. showed that both Resilon/Epiphany and gutta-percha/AH Plus exhibited alternating gap-free and gap-containing regions along canal walls, while silver tracer penetration was detected at the sealer–hybrid layer interface for Resilon/Epiphany and at the sealer–core interface for gutta-percha/AH Plus, leading the authors to conclude that neither system achieved a truly hermetic apical seal ref [6]. These observations are important because they indicate that interfacial continuity in resin-based obturation is technique- and substrate-sensitive rather than intrinsic to the material concept itself.

Apical sealing performance of Resilon also appears to be time dependent. In an ex vivo capillary flow porometry study of root-end fillings, Resilon/Epiphany SE showed smaller pore diameters than gutta-percha/AH 26 and MTA at early time points, suggesting a favorable short-term seal; however, after 6 months its pore dimensions increased, whereas those of gutta-percha and MTA tended to decrease, indicating deterioration of the Resilon seal over time ref [7]. Thus, short-term sealing data may overestimate the long-term clinical promise of the material, particularly when interfacial hydrolytic or polymer-related degradation is considered.

The quality of the apical interface is also influenced by canal pretreatment and obturation conditions. Bodrumlu et al. found that irrigation regimen significantly altered apical sealing outcomes for Resilon/Epiphany SE as well as conventional sealers, with chlorhexidine-associated groups showing greater dye leakage and MTAD showing the least leakage among the tested irrigants ref [9]. Although not a direct seal study, work on thermoplastic obturation further suggests that Resilon can adapt effectively to complex anatomy, including lateral canals when delivered with the Obtura II system ref [12]; this improved filling of accessory spaces should not, however, be conflated with durable nanoscale interfacial sealing. Overall, the literature supports a nuanced view: Resilon may provide acceptable initial adaptation, but ultrastructural and aging studies consistently question whether this translates into a stable apical seal ref [6], ref [7], ref [9].

subsections.section_title: Interfacial Sealing Performance and Microleakage Assessment
subsections.subsection_title: Interfacial Bond Strength to Root Dentin
subsections.content:
Interfacial bond strength to root dentin was central to the original “monoblock” rationale for Resilon/Epiphany, and was most commonly assessed with thin-slice push-out tests. However, the available evidence does not show a consistent bonding advantage over conventional gutta-percha/sealer systems. In a foundational comparison, Gesi et al. found that when premature failures were included, gutta-percha/AH Plus exhibited significantly higher interfacial strength than Resilon/Epiphany; failure in the Resilon group occurred predominantly at the sealer–dentin interface, often with fractured resin tags, indicating that tag formation alone did not ensure durable adhesion ref [10]. Similarly, Rocha et al. reported higher push-out values for AH Plus/gutta-percha than Epiphany/Resilon irrespective of the irrigant used ref [14].

Comparative pairing studies further suggest that bond strength depends at least as much on the sealer–core combination and sealer film behavior as on the Resilon core itself. Ungor et al. showed significant differences among combinations, with Epiphany + gutta-percha producing the highest push-out values, exceeding Epiphany + Resilon and AH Plus + Resilon, whereas gutta-percha alone had negligible resistance ref [11]. Jainaen et al. likewise demonstrated that resin sealers had much higher bond strengths when tested as bulk sealer alone than when used as a thin film around a main cone; for the Resilon sealer, push-out strength dropped markedly in the presence of the cone, underscoring the weakness of the clinically relevant sealer interface ref [7].

Later ex vivo work reinforced this generally modest bonding profile for methacrylate-based Resilon systems. Costa et al. found very low push-out strength for Epiphany-based protocols used with Resilon, whereas Hybrid Root SEAL performed substantially better, with adhesive failures predominating in most Epiphany groups ref [15]. Pawińska et al. also showed that obturation technique influenced interfacial strength, but Resilon/Epiphany did not demonstrate a clear, universal superiority over gutta-percha-based fillings across techniques ref [13]. Overall, the literature indicates that Resilon can bond to radicular dentin in principle, yet this bond is technique-sensitive, often localized to the sealer–dentin interface, and generally insufficient to substantiate claims of meaningful reinforcement of root-filled teeth ref [10], ref [13], ref [15].

subsections.section_title: Interfacial Sealing Performance and Microleakage Assessment
subsections.content:
Microbial leakage studies on Resilon largely used split-chamber models to test whether the putative “monoblock” translates into superior resistance to corono-apical or apico-coronal bacterial penetration. In an influential 30-day model using Streptococcus mutans and Enterococcus faecalis, Resilon/Epiphany showed markedly fewer leakage events than gutta-percha-based controls regardless of whether lateral or vertical condensation was used; by contrast, most gutta-percha specimens leaked during the test period ref [16]. Supporting this trend, Eldeniz and Ørstavik found that Epiphany-filled specimens—used with Resilon rather than gutta-percha—performed significantly better than several conventional and contemporary sealers in a 40-day coronal leakage assay with S. mutans ref [18].

However, the microbial leakage literature is not uniformly favorable. Using E. faecalis inoculation combined with PCR/OCEAN sequence detection, Pasqualini et al. reported more microleakage events for Resilon/Epiphany than for gutta-percha with zinc oxide–eugenol sealer, suggesting that results are sensitive to assay design, obturation extent, and detection method ref [17]. Likewise, when post space was prepared after warm vertical compaction of Resilon/Epiphany, all specimens leaked within 14 days, with no significant difference between immediate and delayed preparation ref [5]. These findings indicate that the sealing advantage of Resilon may be compromised by subsequent restorative procedures or by more sensitive microbial detection strategies.

A related body of work examined saliva leakage rather than single-species challenge. In canals obturated with Resilon/Epiphany Self-Etch, final irrigation with 2% chlorhexidine tended to improve resistance to coronal saliva leakage compared with distilled water, although the difference was not statistically significant over 60 days ref [6]. Overall, bacterial leakage evidence for Resilon is therefore mixed: some ex vivo models show clear short-term superiority over gutta-percha-based fillings, whereas others demonstrate comparable or even inferior resistance under clinically relevant perturbations ref [16], ref [17], ref [5], ref [6]. This inconsistency likely reflects the strong dependence of microbial leakage outcomes on organism selection, chamber configuration, obturation protocol, and post-obturation manipulation.

subsections.section_title: Interfacial Sealing Performance and Microleakage Assessment
subsections.subsection_title: Dye, Fluid, and Glucose-Based Microleakage Models
subsections.content:
Interpretation of Resilon microleakage data depends strongly on the tracer model employed. Dye-based approaches initially suggested favorable sealing for Resilon/Epiphany: spectrophotometric methylene-blue methods found lower leakage than gutta-percha/AH Plus or some other sealer combinations, and no significant difference between active and passive dye challenge was detected in one comparative study ref [20], ref [21]. These findings supported the original monoblock concept, but they also highlighted a general limitation of dye assays: results are highly sensitive to dye chemistry, immersion time, pressure conditions, and quantification strategy.

Fluid-transport models often produced a different ranking. In a longitudinal study, Epiphany/Resilon showed higher leakage than AH Plus/gutta-percha both immediately and after 180 days, irrespective of coronal sealing strategy, although leakage decreased over time in all groups ref [24]. Likewise, when fluid transport and glucose penetration were compared in the same ex vivo design, the fluid model detected no significant difference among groups, whereas the glucose model identified greater leakage for Resilon/Epiphany, particularly after early time points ref [8]. These discrepancies indicate that hydraulic conductance and molecular tracer penetration do not interrogate exactly the same interfacial phenomena.

Glucose-based models were introduced to provide a clinically relevant small-molecule tracer, but they have important methodological caveats. Coronal leakage studies showed measurable glucose passage through filled canals for both Resilon/Epiphany and gutta-percha/AH26, with no leakage through intact root structure and no significant difference between the two materials under the tested conditions ref [7]. However, the reliability of this model is constrained by material–glucose interactions; several endodontic materials can chemically reduce glucose concentration, although Epiphany and Resilon themselves were not among the reactive materials identified in that screening study ref [25]. Overall, the literature suggests that Resilon’s apparent sealing superiority is model-dependent, and conclusions should be weighted toward studies using complementary leakage methods rather than any single assay ref [21], ref [24], ref [8].

Biocompatibility studies on Resilon-based obturation systems indicate a more nuanced profile than simple material equivalence with gutta-percha. In direct cell-culture testing, Resilon showed greater antiproliferative effects than conventional gutta-percha points, with toxicity increasing between 24 and 48 h in both L929 and RPC-C2A cell lines; significant differences became evident particularly after longer exposure, suggesting a time-dependent cytotoxic response rather than acute severe toxicity alone ref [27].

When evaluated in a root model that better simulates clinical diffusion through the apical area, the combination of Resilon and Epiphany was among the most cytotoxic materials during the first 1–2 days, but this effect declined substantially by 7 and 30 days to levels comparable with established sealers ref [28]. Importantly, the same study found that Resilon itself was not cytotoxic under ISO 10993-5 conditions, implicating the methacrylate-based sealer component, especially Epiphany, as the main contributor to early adverse cellular responses ref [28]. This distinction is important because many reports on “Resilon toxicity” actually reflect the behavior of the multicomponent Resilon/Epiphany system rather than the core cone material in isolation.

In vivo evidence generally supports acceptable tissue compatibility, although not complete biological inertness. In rat subcutaneous implantation, RealSeal sealer and primer elicited inflammatory reactions that were mostly comparable to AH Plus and controls over time, but the RealSeal sealer group showed significantly higher lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate at 90 days, indicating that some components may sustain low-grade tissue irritation in the longer term ref [4]. Taken together, the literature suggests that the biocompatibility of Resilon-based obturation depends strongly on the tested configuration, exposure period, and whether the cone material is assessed alone or together with its resin sealer/primer system ref [27], ref [28], ref [4].

Evidence on periapical and tissue repair with Resilon/Epiphany is driven mainly by animal histopathology studies rather than long-term human outcome trials. In a dog-teeth model, Tanomaru-Filho et al. found that canals filled with the Resilon/Epiphany system showed apical and periapical repair comparable to AH Plus and Roeko Seal after 90 days, with significantly better healing than the zinc oxide–eugenol sealer Intrafill; inflammatory infiltrate, mineralized tissue resorption, and apical mineralized tissue deposition were all considered satisfactory for the Epiphany group ref [29]. These findings suggest that, when confined within the canal and used under controlled conditions, the material can support acceptable periapical healing.

However, repair outcomes appear sensitive to the integrity and durability of the filling complex. In a canine model of coronal microbial challenge, roots filled with Resilon were associated with periapical inflammation after contamination, indicating that biological success depends not only on initial biocompatibility but also on maintenance of the seal under functional conditions ref [2]. This is especially relevant because Resilon is a polycaprolactone-based material susceptible to hydrolytic and enzymatic degradation, phenomena that may compromise long-term sealing and thereby secondarily affect periapical repair rather than directly injure tissues ref [3], ref [4].

Taken together, the available literature supports a nuanced interpretation: Resilon/Epiphany can permit satisfactory periapical tissue healing in short-term experimental settings, but its tissue-repair performance is closely tied to interfacial stability and resistance to leakage over time ref [29], ref [2]. Thus, from a biological repair perspective, the system appears acceptable in principle, yet its long-term periapical predictability remains less certain than early histologic compatibility alone would suggest.

The evidence base indicates that Resilon itself does not provide broad intrinsic antimicrobial protection. In an agar diffusion study against Enterococcus faecalis, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, Porphyromonas endodontalis, and Candida albicans, Resilon showed no activity against most tested organisms and only a limited, short-lived effect against S. aureus during the first 24 hours; its antifungal activity was likewise minimal ref [31]. These findings suggest that any microbiological advantage of the Resilon system is unlikely to derive from the core material alone, but rather from canal disinfection before obturation and from the sealer–interface quality that may limit reinfection.

A more clinically relevant issue is chairside decontamination of cones before use. Resilon cones contaminated with E. faecalis were effectively disinfected within 1 minute by sodium hypochlorite and chlorhexidine solutions, although efficacy depended on concentration; the study supports rapid chemical decontamination protocols similar to those used for gutta-percha cones ref [30]. This is important because Resilon is a thermoplastic polymer and cannot be sterilized by heat in routine practice, making chemical disinfection a necessary step when cone contamination is suspected.

Taken together, the available literature portrays Resilon as microbiologically passive rather than actively antimicrobial. Its clinical performance therefore depends primarily on conventional infection-control measures—adequate chemomechanical preparation, use of effective irrigants and intracanal medicaments when indicated, and proper cone disinfection before obturation—rather than on any substantive antibacterial or antifungal effect inherent to the obturating core material ref [30], ref [31].
